In **every** collision, elastic or not, the total linear momentum is conserved.
**Step 1 — see why momentum always survives.** During the collision the two bodies exert
equal and opposite forces on each other for the same time ✓ The impulses are therefore
equal and opposite, so whatever momentum one loses the other gains. With no external
force acting during the brief contact, the total is unchanged.
**Step 2 — see why kinetic energy does not.** "Inelastic" means precisely that some
kinetic energy is **converted** - into heat, sound and permanent deformation ✓ So the
total kinetic energy **falls**, and the total **mechanical** energy with it.
**Step 3 — dismiss the remaining option.** The speed of each body plainly changes in a
collision - that is what a collision is ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** Only the **total linear momentum** is always conserved ✓
**A worked instance.** A 2 kg body at 6 m s⁻¹ strikes a stationary 4 kg body and they
move off together:
momentum: 12 before; after, (6)(2) = **12** ✓ conserved
kinetic energy: ½(2)(36) = **36 J** before; ½(6)(4) = **12 J** after ✗ two thirds lost
**Where the lost energy goes.** Into **heat** in the two bodies, **sound**, and the work
of **deforming** them ✓ Total energy, counting all forms, is of course conserved - it is
the **mechanical** part that is not.
**The three kinds of collision.**
**elastic**: momentum ✓ and kinetic energy ✓ both conserved
**inelastic**: momentum ✓ only
**perfectly inelastic**: momentum ✓ only, with the **maximum** possible energy loss, the
bodies moving off together ✓
**Why this is so useful.** Momentum conservation holds whatever the bodies are made of
and however they deform ✓ It is often the **only** equation available for an inelastic
collision, and it is enough to find the final velocity when the bodies coalesce.
∴ total linear momentum.
pradeep|Physics|0|7|Pradeep Physics · Cl:
Energy conservation fixes the **speeds** as equal; the geometry decides which stone
arrives **first**.
**Step 1 — compare the final speeds.** Both tracks are **frictionless** and both stones
descend the same height h from rest, so by conservation of energy
½mv² = mgh
**v = √(2gh)** for each ✓
The speeds at the bottom are **equal**, whatever the steepness.
**Step 2 — compare the accelerations.** On a slope of angle θ the acceleration along the
track is **g sin θ** ✓ The steeper track, II, has the larger θ, hence the larger
acceleration.
**Step 3 — compare the path lengths.** For the same height h, the length of the track is
L = h/sin θ ✓ The steeper track is also the **shorter** one.
**Step 4 — combine.** Stone II travels a **shorter** distance with a **greater**
acceleration, so it must take less time:
t = √(2L/a) = √(2h/(g sin²θ)) = (1/sin θ)√(2h/g) ✓
A larger θ means a smaller t, so **stone II reaches the bottom earlier** ✓
**Step 5 — conclude.** Same speed, stone II first ✓
**Why the speeds are equal despite the different paths.** Gravity is a **conservative**
force, so the work it does depends only on the **height dropped**, not on the route ✓
This is the same reason the work needed to climb a hill is the same by any smooth path.
**A worked comparison.** With h = 5 m, g = 10 m s⁻²:
both stones arrive at v = √100 = **10 m s⁻¹** ✓
at θ = 30°: t = (1/0·5)√1 = **2·0 s**
at θ = 60°: t = (1/0·866)(1) = **1·15 s** ✓ the steeper track is much quicker.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Same time but not same speed**" ✗ reverses both
conclusions. "**Stone I earlier**" ✗ picks the gentler track, which is longer and slower.
"**Different times and different speeds**" ✗ gets the times right but the speeds wrong ✓
∴ both reach the bottom with the same speed and stone II reaches earlier.
pradeep|Physics|0|10|Pradeep Physics · C:
Use the **work-energy theorem**: the work done by the net force equals the change in
kinetic energy.
**Step 1 — find the speed at each end.** With v = ax^(3/2) and a = 5:
at x = 0: v = **0**
at x = 2: v = 5(2)^(3/2) = 5(2·828) = **14·14 m s⁻¹**
**Step 2 — square it conveniently.**
v² = a²x³ = 25(8) = **200 m² s⁻²**
**Step 3 — apply the work-energy theorem.**
W = ΔKE
= ½mv_f² − ½mv_i²
= ½(0·5)(200) − 0
= **50 J** ✓
**Why no integration of the force is needed.** The work-energy theorem sidesteps the
force entirely ✓ Only the endpoint speeds matter, and the velocity is given as a function
of position - exactly what is required.
**The long route, as a check.** The acceleration is
A = v dv/dx
= (ax^(3/2))(3a/2)x^(1/2)
= (3a²/2)x²
= **37·5x²**
so F = mA = 0·5(37·5x²) = **18·75x²**, and
W = ∫₀² 18·75x² dx
= 18·75[x³/3]₀²
= 18·75(8/3)
= **50 J** ✓ identical, confirming the answer by a wholly independent method.
**Why v dv/dx and not dv/dt.** The velocity is given in terms of **x**, not t ✓ The chain
rule a = dv/dt = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v dv/dx converts it, and this form is the standard
tool whenever velocity is a function of position.
**Checking the units of a.** It is given as m^(−1/2) s⁻¹, so ax^(3/2) has units
m^(−1/2) s⁻¹ x m^(3/2) = **m s⁻¹** ✓ a velocity, as required.
**Reading the distractors.** **1·5 J** ✗ and **10 J** ✗ are far too small - the final
kinetic energy alone is 50 J. **100 J** ✗ omits the factor of ½ in ½mv² ✓
∴ 50 J.

The force follows from the **change in momentum** divided by the contact time.
**Step 1 — convert the speed to SI units.**
126 km/h = 126 x (1000/3600)
= **35 m s⁻¹**
**Step 2 — find the change in momentum.** The collision is elastic and the bat is held
firmly, so the ball rebounds with the **same speed** in the **opposite** direction:
Δp = m[v_final − v_initial]
= 0·150[(+35) − (−35)]
= 0·150(70)
= **10·5 kg m s⁻¹**
**Step 3 — divide by the contact time.**
F = Δp/Δt
= 10·5/0·001
= **1·05 x 10⁴ N** ✓
**Why the factor of 70 and not 35.** The ball's velocity **reverses**, so the change is
twice the speed ✓ Using 35 instead of 70 halves the answer and produces one of the
distractors - this is the single commonest error in impulse problems.
**How large that force is.** 1·05 x 10⁴ N is about **1 tonne-weight** ✓ The batsman feels
it only as a jolt because it lasts a thousandth of a second, but it is why a firmly held
bat is essential and why the hands sting.
**Why the collision time matters so much.** The same momentum change spread over 0·01 s
would give only **1050 N** ✓ This is the principle behind every cushioning device -
airbags, crash helmets, landing mats - all of which extend Δt to reduce F.
**Checking the mass conversion.** 150 g = **0·150 kg** ✓ Leaving it in grams gives
1·05 x 10⁷, a thousand times too large.
**Why "held firmly" matters.** It means the bat does not recoil, so all the momentum
change belongs to the ball ✓ A loosely held bat would move back, lengthening the contact
and reducing both the force and the rebound speed.
**Reading the distractors.** **10·5 N** ✗ and **21 N** ✗ forget to divide by the
0·001 s. **2·1 x 10⁴ N** ✗ doubles the momentum change a second time ✓
∴ 1·05 x 10⁴ N.
